turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_retention_train.csv: 55 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S) and `target` (the measured hot-strength retention ratio
    YS(600C)/YS(20C)).
  - b3_htsteel_retention_pool.csv: 26 CANDIDATE samples whose hot-strength
    retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C) was NOT measured, columns
    `candidate_id` and the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST hot-
strength retention ratio YS(600C)/YS(20C), then select the 5 best candidates
from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
The highest training targets are dominated by two alloy families:

- High‑Ni (≈25–36%) heat‑resistant alloys with Ti/W/Al/B: targets ≈0.82–1.00.
- A matching high‑Ti (≈2.9), Ni≈19–23, B/Al alloy: target ≈0.90.
- High‑Mn/V/Mo grades reach ≈0.80–0.88, while low‑alloy high‑Fe and plain CrNi grades are mostly lower.

Mapping candidates to these clusters:
- c019 ≈ the 1.00/0.875 high‑Ni (35%) + Ti + W + B + Al superalloy family → highest.
- c011 closely matches the 0.903 alloy (Cr≈11.25, Ni≈19–23, Ti≈2.9, B, Al).
- c013 and c004 match the 0.821–0.875 high‑Ni/Ti/B/Al family (c013 also has W; c004 has extra Mo but no W).
- c008 is essentially identical to a training row with target ≈0.696, edging out c018/c005/c009 (~0.63–0.68).

Final: c019, c011, c013, c004, c008
